He completed a late-race pass to claim victory and has won the last four IndyCar oval races leading up to that date.

So the answer is: **Josef Newgarden**.

_**Jazz Portraits: Mingus in Wonderland**_ is a live album by the jazz bassist and composer Charles Mingus, recorded in 1959 and released on the United Artists label in September of that year.[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jazz_Portraits:_Mingus_in_Wonderland#cite_note-CashBox-1)[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jazz_Portraits:_Mingus_in_Wonderland#cite_note-Billboard-2)[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jazz_Portraits:_Mingus_in_Wonderland#cite_note-Charles_Mingus_discography-3) The original release was titled _**Jazz Portraits**_, and a subsequent edition was titled _**Wonderland**_, leading to the combined title of _**Jazz Portraits: Mingus in Wonderland**_.

Both "Alice's Wonderland" and "Nostalgia in Times Square" were originally written for the 1959 John Cassavetes film _Shadows_ as part of a complete soundtrack. However, Mingus’ music was largely replaced in the final version of the film. A partial reconstruction of the soundtrack was released in 2015 as the compilation album _Shadows_.
A reworked version of "Nostalgia in Times Square," featuring vocals by Honi Gordon, was recorded during Mingus' 1959 _Mingus Dynasty_ sessions and included as a bonus track on reissues of that album, titled "Strollin'".
Although "Nostalgia in Times Square" was never a major part of Mingus’ repertoire, it has since become a jazz standard, widely performed and recorded by other musicians.[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jazz_Portraits:_Mingus_in_Wonderland#cite_note-4) Notably, the jazz fusion trio Medeski Martin & Wood frequently perform the song, often as part of a medley with Sun Ra’s “Angel Race.”[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jazz_Portraits:_Mingus_in_Wonderland#cite_note-5)
The AllMusic review by Scott Yanow called the music "advanced bop that looks toward the upcoming innovations of the avant-garde and is frequently quite exciting".[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jazz_Portraits:_Mingus_in_Wonderland#cite_note-Allmusic-6)

Title: ON THIS DAY, 1959: Mingus Jazz Workshop records at the Nonagon Gallery — CHARLES MINGUS
Chunks: 0,1
“One bitter night between sets at the Five Spot, Charles Mingus told his sidemen to pack their gear and follow him through the icy slush a few blocks to the Nonagon Art Gallery.” (Gene Santoro, _Myself When I Am Real: The Life and Music of Charles Mingus_)
We received a lot of interest on our recent social media posts about Mingus’ New Year’s Eve engagement at the end of 1958 amid his famed residency at the Five Spot. Sadly, no recordings of those performances are known to exist, but Mingus did document this group on January 16th, 1959, immediately between two sets of music at the Five Spot. It was to be the first of four historic recordings made by the bandleader during jazz’s most famous landmark year. Produced by Nat Hentoff, the album was released by United Artists as _Jazz Portraits_ (later re-titled _Jazz Portraits: Mingus In Wonderland_). In addition to Mingus on bass, the Jazz Workshop featured John Handy, Booker Ervin, Richard Wyands, and Dannie Richmond.
Two of the Mingus compositions heard here debuted in 1958 as part of the soundtrack for the John Cassavetes film _Shadows,_ though much of the bassist’s contributions were ultimately omitted from the revised 1959 version of the film. At the Nonagon Gallery event, additional songs were performed but left off the album, including “Take the ‘A’ Train,” “Jelly Roll Jollies” (aka “My Jelly Roll Soul”), “Billie’s Bounce,” and “Wednesday Night Prayer Meeting.” Admission to the event was $2, and the musicians were compensated $24.54 apiece. During the editing process, Mingus remarked “You know, I think maybe I’m finally composing.”

(2) Charles Mingus, John Handy, Booker Ervin during a performance at the Five Spot, 1958 (Photo: Dennis Stock)
(3) Nonagon Gallery, 1959 (on a different date from the Mingus performance) (Photo: Fred W. McDarrah)

_**Jazz Portraits: Mingus in Wonderland**_ is a live album by the jazz bassist and composer Charles Mingus, recorded in 1959 and released on the United Artists label in September of that year.[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jazz_Portraits:_Mingus_in_Wonderland#cite_note-CashBox-1)[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jazz_Portraits:_Mingus_in_Wonderland#cite_note-Billboard-2)[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jazz_Portraits:_Mingus_in_Wonderland#cite_note-Charles_Mingus_discography-3) The original release was titled _**Jazz Portraits**_, and a subsequent edition was titled _**Wonderland**_, leading to the combined title of _**Jazz Portraits: Mingus in Wonderland**_.

Both "Alice's Wonderland" and "Nostalgia in Times Square" were originally written for the 1959 John Cassavetes film _Shadows_ as part of a complete soundtrack. However, Mingus’ music was largely replaced in the final version of the film. A partial reconstruction of the soundtrack was released in 2015 as the compilation album _Shadows_.
A reworked version of "Nostalgia in Times Square," featuring vocals by Honi Gordon, was recorded during Mingus' 1959 _Mingus Dynasty_ sessions and included as a bonus track on reissues of that album, titled "Strollin'".
Although "Nostalgia in Times Square" was never a major part of Mingus’ repertoire, it has since become a jazz standard, widely performed and recorded by other musicians.[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jazz_Portraits:_Mingus_in_Wonderland#cite_note-4) Notably, the jazz fusion trio Medeski Martin & Wood frequently perform the song, often as part of a medley with Sun Ra’s “Angel Race.”[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jazz_Portraits:_Mingus_in_Wonderland#cite_note-5)
The AllMusic review by Scott Yanow called the music "advanced bop that looks toward the upcoming innovations of the avant-garde and is frequently quite exciting".[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jazz_Portraits:_Mingus_in_Wonderland#cite_note-Allmusic-6)

“One bitter night between sets at the Five Spot, Charles Mingus told his sidemen to pack their gear and follow him through the icy slush a few blocks to the Nonagon Art Gallery.” (Gene Santoro, _Myself When I Am Real: The Life and Music of Charles Mingus_)
We received a lot of interest on our recent social media posts about Mingus’ New Year’s Eve engagement at the end of 1958 amid his famed residency at the Five Spot. Sadly, no recordings of those performances are known to exist, but Mingus did document this group on January 16th, 1959, immediately between two sets of music at the Five Spot. It was to be the first of four historic recordings made by the bandleader during jazz’s most famous landmark year. Produced by Nat Hentoff, the album was released by United Artists as _Jazz Portraits_ (later re-titled _Jazz Portraits: Mingus In Wonderland_). In addition to Mingus on bass, the Jazz Workshop featured John Handy, Booker Ervin, Richard Wyands, and Dannie Richmond.
Two of the Mingus compositions heard here debuted in 1958 as part of the soundtrack for the John Cassavetes film _Shadows,_ though much of the bassist’s contributions were ultimately omitted from the revised 1959 version of the film. At the Nonagon Gallery event, additional songs were performed but left off the album, including “Take the ‘A’ Train,” “Jelly Roll Jollies” (aka “My Jelly Roll Soul”), “Billie’s Bounce,” and “Wednesday Night Prayer Meeting.” Admission to the event was $2, and the musicians were compensated $24.54 apiece. During the editing process, Mingus remarked “You know, I think maybe I’m finally composing.”

_**Jazz Portraits: Mingus in Wonderland**_ is a live album by the jazz bassist and composer Charles Mingus, recorded in 1959 and released on the United Artists label in September of that year.[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jazz_Portraits:_Mingus_in_Wonderland#cite_note-CashBox-1)[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jazz_Portraits:_Mingus_in_Wonderland#cite_note-Billboard-2)[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jazz_Portraits:_Mingus_in_Wonderland#cite_note-Charles_Mingus_discography-3) The original release was titled _**Jazz Portraits**_, and a subsequent edition was titled _**Wonderland**_, leading to the combined title of _**Jazz Portraits: Mingus in Wonderland**_.

Both "Alice's Wonderland" and "Nostalgia in Times Square" were originally written for the 1959 John Cassavetes film _Shadows_ as part of a complete soundtrack. However, Mingus’ music was largely replaced in the final version of the film. A partial reconstruction of the soundtrack was released in 2015 as the compilation album _Shadows_.
A reworked version of "Nostalgia in Times Square," featuring vocals by Honi Gordon, was recorded during Mingus' 1959 _Mingus Dynasty_ sessions and included as a bonus track on reissues of that album, titled "Strollin'".
Although "Nostalgia in Times Square" was never a major part of Mingus’ repertoire, it has since become a jazz standard, widely performed and recorded by other musicians.[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jazz_Portraits:_Mingus_in_Wonderland#cite_note-4) Notably, the jazz fusion trio Medeski Martin & Wood frequently perform the song, often as part of a medley with Sun Ra’s “Angel Race.”[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jazz_Portraits:_Mingus_in_Wonderland#cite_note-5)
The AllMusic review by Scott Yanow called the music "advanced bop that looks toward the upcoming innovations of the avant-garde and is frequently quite exciting".[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jazz_Portraits:_Mingus_in_Wonderland#cite_note-Allmusic-6)

Title: ON THIS DAY, 1959: Mingus Jazz Workshop records at the Nonagon Gallery — CHARLES MINGUS
Chunks: 0,1
“One bitter night between sets at the Five Spot, Charles Mingus told his sidemen to pack their gear and follow him through the icy slush a few blocks to the Nonagon Art Gallery.” (Gene Santoro, _Myself When I Am Real: The Life and Music of Charles Mingus_)
We received a lot of interest on our recent social media posts about Mingus’ New Year’s Eve engagement at the end of 1958 amid his famed residency at the Five Spot. Sadly, no recordings of those performances are known to exist, but Mingus did document this group on January 16th, 1959, immediately between two sets of music at the Five Spot. It was to be the first of four historic recordings made by the bandleader during jazz’s most famous landmark year. Produced by Nat Hentoff, the album was released by United Artists as _Jazz Portraits_ (later re-titled _Jazz Portraits: Mingus In Wonderland_). In addition to Mingus on bass, the Jazz Workshop featured John Handy, Booker Ervin, Richard Wyands, and Dannie Richmond.
Two of the Mingus compositions heard here debuted in 1958 as part of the soundtrack for the John Cassavetes film _Shadows,_ though much of the bassist’s contributions were ultimately omitted from the revised 1959 version of the film. At the Nonagon Gallery event, additional songs were performed but left off the album, including “Take the ‘A’ Train,” “Jelly Roll Jollies” (aka “My Jelly Roll Soul”), “Billie’s Bounce,” and “Wednesday Night Prayer Meeting.” Admission to the event was $2, and the musicians were compensated $24.54 apiece. During the editing process, Mingus remarked “You know, I think maybe I’m finally composing.”

**Charles Mingus Jr.** (April 22, 1922 – January 5, 1979) was an American jazzupright bassist, composer, bandleader, pianist, and author. A major proponent of collective improvisation, he is considered one of the greatest jazz musicians and composers in history,[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Charles_Mingus#cite_note-Underdog-1) with a career spanning three decades and collaborations with other jazz greats, such as Duke Ellington, Charlie Parker, Max Roach, and Eric Dolphy. Mingus's work ranged from advanced bebop and avant-garde jazz with small and midsize ensembles to pioneering the post-bop style on seminal recordings like _Pithecanthropus Erectus_ (1956) and _Mingus Ah Um_ (1959) and progressive big band experiments such as _The Black Saint and the Sinner Lady_ (1963).

Mingus's compositions continue to be played by contemporary musicians ranging from the repertory bands Mingus Big Band, Mingus Dynasty, and Mingus Orchestra to high school students who play the charts and compete in the Charles Mingus High School Competition.[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Charles_Mingus#cite_note-2) In 1993, the Library of Congress acquired Mingus's collected papers—including scores, sound recordings, correspondence, and photos—in what it called "the most important acquisition of a manuscript collection relating to jazz in the Library's history".[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Charles_Mingus#cite_note-3)

### Early life and career
[edit]
Mingus was born in Nogales, Arizona, in 1922, to Charles Mingus Sr., a staff sergeant in the U.S. Army, and Harriet Sophia Mingus (née Phillips). His family moved to the Watts area of Los Angeles shortly after his birth.[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Charles_Mingus#cite_note-FOOTNOTESantoro2000b13%E2%80%9314-4)
Charles Sr. was born in 1877 in Swain County, North Carolina, in the Great Smoky Mountains. His mother was a white teenager, Clarinda Mingus; his father was Daniel Mingus, a farmhand and former slave who worked for Clarinda's family. Clarinda married and started a new family when he was six, leaving him in the care of her father and grandparents.[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Charles_Mingus#cite_note-5) He left home at fourteen, enlisting in the army and seeing action in the Spanish–American War. In 1917, he married Harriet Sophia Phillips, who was of mixed Chinese and African-American descent. She died of myocarditis in 1922, a few months after the birth of their son.[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Charles_Mingus#cite_note-FOOTNOTESantoro2000b14%E2%80%9317-6)

### Early life and career
Mingus was raised alongside his two elder half-sisters, from his father's first marriage. His father was married for a third time in 1923, to Mamie Carson.[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Charles_Mingus#cite_note-FOOTNOTESantoro2000b18-7) Mamie allowed only church-related music in their home, but Mingus developed an early love for other music, especially that of Duke Ellington. He studied trombone, and later cello, although he was unable to follow the cello professionally because, at the time, it was nearly impossible for a black musician to make a career of classical music, and the cello was not accepted as a jazz instrument. Despite this, Mingus remained attached to the cello; as he studied bass with Red Callender in the late 1930s, Callender even commented that the cello was still Mingus's main instrument. In his autobiography, _Beneath the Underdog_, Mingus states that he did not actually start learning bass until Buddy Collette accepted him into his swing band under the stipulation that he be the band's bass player.[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Charles_Mingus#cite_note-autogenerated1991-8)
Due to a poor education, the young Mingus could not read musical notation quickly enough to join the local youth orchestra. This had a serious impact on his early musical experiences, leaving him feeling ostracized from the classical music world. These early experiences, in addition to his lifelong confrontations with racism, were reflected in his music, which often focused on themes of racism, discrimination, and (in)justice.[[9]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Charles_Mingus#cite_note-Horton-9)
Much of the cello technique Mingus learned was applicable to double bass when he took up the instrument in high school. He studied for five years with Herman Reinshagen, principal bassist of the New York Philharmonic, and compositional techniques with Lloyd Reese.[[10]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Charles_Mingus#cite_note-10) Throughout much of his career, he played a bass made in 1927 by the German maker Ernst Heinrich Roth.

### Early life and career
Mingus was already writing relatively advanced musical pieces in his teenage years; many are similar to third stream in that they incorporate elements of classical music. A number of pieces of his were recorded in 1960 with conductor Gunther Schuller and released as _Pre-Bird_, referring to Charlie "Bird" Parker; Mingus was one of many musicians whose perspectives on music were altered by Parker into "pre- and post-Bird" eras._[citation needed_]
Mingus gained a reputation as a bass prodigy. His first major professional job was playing with former Ellington clarinetist Barney Bigard. He toured with Louis Armstrong in 1943, and by early 1945 was recording in Los Angeles in a band led by Russell Jacquet, which also included Teddy Edwards, Maurice James Simon, Wild Bill Davis, and Chico Hamilton. In May that year, in Hollywood, he was again with Edwards, in a band led by Howard McGhee.[[11]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Charles_Mingus#cite_note-11)
He then played with Lionel Hampton's band in the late 1940s; Hampton performed and recorded several Mingus pieces. In 1950–51, a popular trio of Mingus, Red Norvo and Tal Farlow, received considerable acclaim, but Mingus's race caused problems with some club owners and he left the group. Mingus was briefly a member of Ellington's band in 1953, as a substitute for bassist Wendell Marshall; however, Mingus's notorious temper led to his being one of the few musicians personally fired by Ellington ([Bubber Miley](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/James_%22Bubber%22_Miley "James \"Bubber\" Miley") and drummer Bobby Durham are among the others) after a backstage fight between Mingus and Juan Tizol.[[12]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Charles_Mingus#cite_note-FOOTNOTEHentoff197834%E2%80%9335-12)

_"Making the simple complicated is commonplace; making the complicated simple, awesomely simple, that's creativity."-_ Charles Mingus
Charles Mingus was one of the most important musicians in the history of jazz. Aside from being an influential bassist whose virtuoso solos and progressive harmonics helped move the bass away from being a simple rhythmic instrument he was a visionary multi-instrumentalist and composer. Influenced by Duke Ellington, Mingus’ work blended the compositional clarity of earlier swing composers with the improvisational freedom that had arrived with bebop. In a series of remarkable albums from the late 1950s to the mid 1960s Mingus laid the foundation for much of what would become avant-garde jazz and his influence was felt, and absorbed, by artists of all musical genres.

### From Cello to Bass
Born in Arizona 1922, Mingus grew up in a home where the only music allowed to be heard was gospel and church songs, an early musical education that would be echoed in many of his later compositions – exemplified by the magnificent _Wednesday Night Prayer Meeting_ in the playlist below. He initially learned the trombone and later moved to the cello, finally switching to bass when he realised that it would be almost impossible, as a black man in the classical music world of the period, to build a professional career as a cellist.
He proved to be an immensely talented bassist and soon found touring work with Louis Armstrong and Lionel Hampton. By the 1950s he’d moved to New York where his playing was held in such high regard that he was performing with musicians including Charlie Parker and Miles Davis. In his autobiography Miles would state, “He was a great bass player. But he was hard to get along with, especially about music, because he had his own definite ideas about what was good and what was bad, and he didn’t mind telling anybody what he had on his mind.” This single-mindedness would cause Mingus to gain a reputation as being difficult and demanding. His vision was certainly too focussed to cut it as a long term side-man and he set out to have more control over his music

### The Jazz Workshop
The idea for the “jazz workshop” had its roots in the “classical workshops” that Mingus attended in the 1940s whilst studying at Los Angeles City College. There he took part in group sessions where musicians could exchange ideas and develop new compositions. He brought the concept with him to New York and by the mid 1950s he had established a loose group of musicians that would work intensely on innovative interpretations of standards and, more importantly, help Mingus develop his own compositions.
Although the spark for the workshop was the idea of collaborative experimentation, Mingus’ forceful personality and passionate intensity guided the group towards his vision of what jazz could be. Some musicians regarded the workshop sessions as being a “university of jazz” while others, mindful of Mingus’ relentless pursuit of perfection, dubbed them “jazz sweatshops”. The workshop process would result in many of Mingus’ classic albums including _Pithecanthropus Erectus_, _The Clown_ and his first masterpiece _Ah Um_.

### The Angry Man of Jazz
Mingus’ volatile personality and the demands he placed on both fellow musicians and his audiences led him to be nicknamed “the angry man of jazz”. There are numerous stories of Mingus’ explosive temper derailing his relationships with previously willing collaborators. In 1963 Mingus punched trombonist Jimmy Knepper so hard that he broke his teeth and he was charged with assault. It was not unheard of for Mingus to halt a concert to berate the audience for making too much noise or not paying proper attention or even to fire a musician mid-set.
While much of his anger can be explained by Mingus’ frustration in not being able to get other musicians to conform to his very particular vision of how his music should be performed it was also fed by bouts of clinical depression and, importantly, a sense of injustice that he had faced discrimination on the basis of his colour for his whole life. Though Mingus would not ally himself to any particular political group, his work during the 1960s in particular, is inherently political, imbued with righteous anger against racism and injustice. Mingus was also an outspoken critic of the music industry itself and in particular the imbalance between the musicians and their record labels often having to fight for royalties and artistic freedom. On one occasion Mingus claimed to have stormed the offices of Columbia Records dressed in a pith helmet and safari suit, brandishing a shotgun and demanding his royalties. An act he described as “creative anger”.

### Cats and Dogs
Mingus’ extraordinary autobiography _Beneath The Underdog_, published in 1971, a freewheeling mix of memoir, fantasy, musical manifesto and personal contemplation is rightly considered one of the classic jazz books. But Mingus’ literary ambitions went beyond the biography. Aside from the extensive and informative sleeve notes he provided for many of his albums, including the Grammy award winning essay “_What Is A Jazz Composer?_” which appeared on the cover of _Let My Children Hear Music_ he also published a rather unusual booklet giving guidance to toilet training cats. Offered for sale at performances or via mail-order _The Charles Mingus CAT-alog_ detailed how he managed to train his cat Nightlife to forego a litter tray and use human facilities. Mingus managed to train his cat in three or four weeks, probably showing more patience with the cat than he had with many of the musicians he worked with.

# Charles Mingus
composer
Follow Artist
One of the most important figures in 20th-century American music, CHARLES MINGUS was a virtuoso bass player, accomplished pianist, bandleader, and composer. Born in Arizona and raised in Watts, California, he studied double bass and composition in a formal way (five years with H. Rheinshagen, principal bassist of the New York Philharmonic, and compositional techniques with the legendary Lloyd Reese) while absorbing vernacular music from the great jazz masters, first-hand. His early professional experience, in the '40s, found him touring with bands like Louis Armstrong, Kid Ory, and Lionel Hampton and brought him to New York where he played and recorded with the leading musicians of the 1950s - Charlie Parker, Miles Davis, Bud Powell, Art Tatum, and Duke Ellington. One of the few bassists to do so, Mingus quickly developed as a leader of musicians, and recorded over a hundred albums and wrote over three hundred scores.
After his death in 1979 from Amyotrophic Lateral Sclerosis, the National Endowment for the Arts provided grants for a Mingus foundation called "Let My Children Hear Music," which catalogued all of Mingus' works. The microfilms of these works were then given to the Music Division of the New York Public Library, where they are currently available for study and scholarship. The Library of Congress acquired the complete Mingus Collection between 1993 and 1997, including original manuscripts, recordings, photographs, and personal memorabilia. The New Yorker wrote: "For sheer melodic and rhythmic and structural originality, his compositions may equal anything written in western music in the 20th century."

# Charles Mingus
Since Charles Mingus' death in 1979, SUE MINGUS has created and continues to direct repertory ensembles to carry on the music of her late husband. The most well-known is the Mingus Big Band, a New York institution that performs weekly to packed crowds at the Iridium nightclub. In 1989, she produced the premiere of Mingus' Epitaph at Lincoln Center's Alice Tully Hall. Other bands include the Mingus Dynasty, the original, seven-piece ensemble founded shortly after Mingus' death, and the Orchestra, a ten-piece ensemble with more classical instrumentation. She has produced numerous Grammy-nominated recordings with all three repertory bands as well as several legacy recordings, including a previously unavailable concert Charles Mingus performed with Eric Dolphy at Cornell University in 1964, available this summer on Blue Note.
Sue's memoir of her life with Mingus, Tonight At Noon, is available in paperback from DaCapo press and has been translated into several languages.

_"Making the simple complicated is commonplace; making the complicated simple, awesomely simple, that's creativity."-_ Charles Mingus
Charles Mingus was one of the most important musicians in the history of jazz. Aside from being an influential bassist whose virtuoso solos and progressive harmonics helped move the bass away from being a simple rhythmic instrument he was a visionary multi-instrumentalist and composer. Influenced by Duke Ellington, Mingus’ work blended the compositional clarity of earlier swing composers with the improvisational freedom that had arrived with bebop. In a series of remarkable albums from the late 1950s to the mid 1960s Mingus laid the foundation for much of what would become avant-garde jazz and his influence was felt, and absorbed, by artists of all musical genres.
texts.1:
### From Cello to Bass
Born in Arizona 1922, Mingus grew up in a home where the only music allowed to be heard was gospel and church songs, an early musical education that would be echoed in many of his later compositions – exemplified by the magnificent _Wednesday Night Prayer Meeting_ in the playlist below. He initially learned the trombone and later moved to the cello, finally switching to bass when he realised that it would be almost impossible, as a black man in the classical music world of the period, to build a professional career as a cellist.
He proved to be an immensely talented bassist and soon found touring work with Louis Armstrong and Lionel Hampton. By the 1950s he’d moved to New York where his playing was held in such high regard that he was performing with musicians including Charlie Parker and Miles Davis. In his autobiography Miles would state, “He was a great bass player. But he was hard to get along with, especially about music, because he had his own definite ideas about what was good and what was bad, and he didn’t mind telling anybody what he had on his mind.” This single-mindedness would cause Mingus to gain a reputation as being difficult and demanding. His vision was certainly too focussed to cut it as a long term side-man and he set out to have more control over his music
texts.2:
### The Jazz Workshop
The idea for the “jazz workshop” had its roots in the “classical workshops” that Mingus attended in the 1940s whilst studying at Los Angeles City College. There he took part in group sessions where musicians could exchange ideas and develop new compositions. He brought the concept with him to New York and by the mid 1950s he had established a loose group of musicians that would work intensely on innovative interpretations of standards and, more importantly, help Mingus develop his own compositions.
Although the spark for the workshop was the idea of collaborative experimentation, Mingus’ forceful personality and passionate intensity guided the group towards his vision of what jazz could be. Some musicians regarded the workshop sessions as being a “university of jazz” while others, mindful of Mingus’ relentless pursuit of perfection, dubbed them “jazz sweatshops”. The workshop process would result in many of Mingus’ classic albums including _Pithecanthropus Erectus_, _The Clown_ and his first masterpiece _Ah Um_.
texts.3:
### The Angry Man of Jazz
Mingus’ volatile personality and the demands he placed on both fellow musicians and his audiences led him to be nicknamed “the angry man of jazz”. There are numerous stories of Mingus’ explosive temper derailing his relationships with previously willing collaborators. In 1963 Mingus punched trombonist Jimmy Knepper so hard that he broke his teeth and he was charged with assault. It was not unheard of for Mingus to halt a concert to berate the audience for making too much noise or not paying proper attention or even to fire a musician mid-set.
While much of his anger can be explained by Mingus’ frustration in not being able to get other musicians to conform to his very particular vision of how his music should be performed it was also fed by bouts of clinical depression and, importantly, a sense of injustice that he had faced discrimination on the basis of his colour for his whole life. Though Mingus would not ally himself to any particular political group, his work during the 1960s in particular, is inherently political, imbued with righteous anger against racism and injustice. Mingus was also an outspoken critic of the music industry itself and in particular the imbalance between the musicians and their record labels often having to fight for royalties and artistic freedom. On one occasion Mingus claimed to have stormed the offices of Columbia Records dressed in a pith helmet and safari suit, brandishing a shotgun and demanding his royalties. An act he described as “creative anger”.
texts.4:
### Cats and Dogs
Mingus’ extraordinary autobiography _Beneath The Underdog_, published in 1971, a freewheeling mix of memoir, fantasy, musical manifesto and personal contemplation is rightly considered one of the classic jazz books. But Mingus’ literary ambitions went beyond the biography. Aside from the extensive and informative sleeve notes he provided for many of his albums, including the Grammy award winning essay “_What Is A Jazz Composer?_” which appeared on the cover of _Let My Children Hear Music_ he also published a rather unusual booklet giving guidance to toilet training cats. Offered for sale at performances or via mail-order _The Charles Mingus CAT-alog_ detailed how he managed to train his cat Nightlife to forego a litter tray and use human facilities. Mingus managed to train his cat in three or four weeks, probably showing more patience with the cat than he had with many of the musicians he worked with.

After his death in 1979 from Amyotrophic Lateral Sclerosis, the National Endowment for the Arts provided grants for a Mingus foundation called "Let My Children Hear Music," which catalogued all of Mingus' works. The microfilms of these works were then given to the Music Division of the New York Public Library, where they are currently available for study and scholarship. The Library of Congress acquired the complete Mingus Collection between 1993 and 1997, including original manuscripts, recordings, photographs, and personal memorabilia. The New Yorker wrote: "For sheer melodic and rhythmic and structural originality, his compositions may equal anything written in western music in the 20th century."

# Charles Mingus
Since Charles Mingus' death in 1979, SUE MINGUS has created and continues to direct repertory ensembles to carry on the music of her late husband. The most well-known is the Mingus Big Band, a New York institution that performs weekly to packed crowds at the Iridium nightclub. In 1989, she produced the premiere of Mingus' Epitaph at Lincoln Center's Alice Tully Hall. Other bands include the Mingus Dynasty, the original, seven-piece ensemble founded shortly after Mingus' death, and the Orchestra, a ten-piece ensemble with more classical instrumentation. She has produced numerous Grammy-nominated recordings with all three repertory bands as well as several legacy recordings, including a previously unavailable concert Charles Mingus performed with Eric Dolphy at Cornell University in 1964, available this summer on Blue Note.
Sue's memoir of her life with Mingus, Tonight At Noon, is available in paperback from DaCapo press and has been translated into several languages.

**Charles Mingus Jr.** (April 22, 1922 – January 5, 1979) was an American jazzupright bassist, composer, bandleader, pianist, and author. A major proponent of collective improvisation, he is considered one of the greatest jazz musicians and composers in history,[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Charles_Mingus#cite_note-Underdog-1) with a career spanning three decades and collaborations with other jazz greats, such as Duke Ellington, Charlie Parker, Max Roach, and Eric Dolphy. Mingus's work ranged from advanced bebop and avant-garde jazz with small and midsize ensembles to pioneering the post-bop style on seminal recordings like _Pithecanthropus Erectus_ (1956) and _Mingus Ah Um_ (1959) and progressive big band experiments such as _The Black Saint and the Sinner Lady_ (1963).
texts.1: Mingus's compositions continue to be played by contemporary musicians ranging from the repertory bands Mingus Big Band, Mingus Dynasty, and Mingus Orchestra to high school students who play the charts and compete in the Charles Mingus High School Competition.[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Charles_Mingus#cite_note-2) In 1993, the Library of Congress acquired Mingus's collected papers—including scores, sound recordings, correspondence, and photos—in what it called "the most important acquisition of a manuscript collection relating to jazz in the Library's history".[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Charles_Mingus#cite_note-3)
texts.2:
### Early life and career
[edit]
Mingus was born in Nogales, Arizona, in 1922, to Charles Mingus Sr., a staff sergeant in the U.S. Army, and Harriet Sophia Mingus (née Phillips). His family moved to the Watts area of Los Angeles shortly after his birth.[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Charles_Mingus#cite_note-FOOTNOTESantoro2000b13%E2%80%9314-4)
Charles Sr. was born in 1877 in Swain County, North Carolina, in the Great Smoky Mountains. His mother was a white teenager, Clarinda Mingus; his father was Daniel Mingus, a farmhand and former slave who worked for Clarinda's family. Clarinda married and started a new family when he was six, leaving him in the care of her father and grandparents.[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Charles_Mingus#cite_note-5) He left home at fourteen, enlisting in the army and seeing action in the Spanish–American War. In 1917, he married Harriet Sophia Phillips, who was of mixed Chinese and African-American descent. She died of myocarditis in 1922, a few months after the birth of their son.[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Charles_Mingus#cite_note-FOOTNOTESantoro2000b14%E2%80%9317-6)
texts.3:
### Early life and career
Mingus was raised alongside his two elder half-sisters, from his father's first marriage. His father was married for a third time in 1923, to Mamie Carson.[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Charles_Mingus#cite_note-FOOTNOTESantoro2000b18-7) Mamie allowed only church-related music in their home, but Mingus developed an early love for other music, especially that of Duke Ellington. He studied trombone, and later cello, although he was unable to follow the cello professionally because, at the time, it was nearly impossible for a black musician to make a career of classical music, and the cello was not accepted as a jazz instrument. Despite this, Mingus remained attached to the cello; as he studied bass with Red Callender in the late 1930s, Callender even commented that the cello was still Mingus's main instrument. In his autobiography, _Beneath the Underdog_, Mingus states that he did not actually start learning bass until Buddy Collette accepted him into his swing band under the stipulation that he be the band's bass player.[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Charles_Mingus#cite_note-autogenerated1991-8)
Due to a poor education, the young Mingus could not read musical notation quickly enough to join the local youth orchestra. This had a serious impact on his early musical experiences, leaving him feeling ostracized from the classical music world. These early experiences, in addition to his lifelong confrontations with racism, were reflected in his music, which often focused on themes of racism, discrimination, and (in)justice.[[9]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Charles_Mingus#cite_note-Horton-9)
Much of the cello technique Mingus learned was applicable to double bass when he took up the instrument in high school. He studied for five years with Herman Reinshagen, principal bassist of the New York Philharmonic, and compositional techniques with Lloyd Reese.[[10]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Charles_Mingus#cite_note-10) Throughout much of his career, he played a bass made in 1927 by the German maker Ernst Heinrich Roth.
texts.4:
### Early life and career
Mingus was already writing relatively advanced musical pieces in his teenage years; many are similar to third stream in that they incorporate elements of classical music. A number of pieces of his were recorded in 1960 with conductor Gunther Schuller and released as _Pre-Bird_, referring to Charlie "Bird" Parker; Mingus was one of many musicians whose perspectives on music were altered by Parker into "pre- and post-Bird" eras._[citation needed_]
Mingus gained a reputation as a bass prodigy. His first major professional job was playing with former Ellington clarinetist Barney Bigard. He toured with Louis Armstrong in 1943, and by early 1945 was recording in Los Angeles in a band led by Russell Jacquet, which also included Teddy Edwards, Maurice James Simon, Wild Bill Davis, and Chico Hamilton. In May that year, in Hollywood, he was again with Edwards, in a band led by Howard McGhee.[[11]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Charles_Mingus#cite_note-11)
He then played with Lionel Hampton's band in the late 1940s; Hampton performed and recorded several Mingus pieces. In 1950–51, a popular trio of Mingus, Red Norvo and Tal Farlow, received considerable acclaim, but Mingus's race caused problems with some club owners and he left the group. Mingus was briefly a member of Ellington's band in 1953, as a substitute for bassist Wendell Marshall; however, Mingus's notorious temper led to his being one of the few musicians personally fired by Ellington ([Bubber Miley](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/James_%22Bubber%22_Miley "James \"Bubber\" Miley") and drummer Bobby Durham are among the others) after a backstage fight between Mingus and Juan Tizol.[[12]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Charles_Mingus#cite_note-FOOTNOTEHentoff197834%E2%80%9335-12)

_"Making the simple complicated is commonplace; making the complicated simple, awesomely simple, that's creativity."-_ Charles Mingus
Charles Mingus was one of the most important musicians in the history of jazz. Aside from being an influential bassist whose virtuoso solos and progressive harmonics helped move the bass away from being a simple rhythmic instrument he was a visionary multi-instrumentalist and composer. Influenced by Duke Ellington, Mingus’ work blended the compositional clarity of earlier swing composers with the improvisational freedom that had arrived with bebop. In a series of remarkable albums from the late 1950s to the mid 1960s Mingus laid the foundation for much of what would become avant-garde jazz and his influence was felt, and absorbed, by artists of all musical genres.

### From Cello to Bass
Born in Arizona 1922, Mingus grew up in a home where the only music allowed to be heard was gospel and church songs, an early musical education that would be echoed in many of his later compositions – exemplified by the magnificent _Wednesday Night Prayer Meeting_ in the playlist below. He initially learned the trombone and later moved to the cello, finally switching to bass when he realised that it would be almost impossible, as a black man in the classical music world of the period, to build a professional career as a cellist.
He proved to be an immensely talented bassist and soon found touring work with Louis Armstrong and Lionel Hampton. By the 1950s he’d moved to New York where his playing was held in such high regard that he was performing with musicians including Charlie Parker and Miles Davis. In his autobiography Miles would state, “He was a great bass player. But he was hard to get along with, especially about music, because he had his own definite ideas about what was good and what was bad, and he didn’t mind telling anybody what he had on his mind.” This single-mindedness would cause Mingus to gain a reputation as being difficult and demanding. His vision was certainly too focussed to cut it as a long term side-man and he set out to have more control over his music

### The Jazz Workshop
The idea for the “jazz workshop” had its roots in the “classical workshops” that Mingus attended in the 1940s whilst studying at Los Angeles City College. There he took part in group sessions where musicians could exchange ideas and develop new compositions. He brought the concept with him to New York and by the mid 1950s he had established a loose group of musicians that would work intensely on innovative interpretations of standards and, more importantly, help Mingus develop his own compositions.
Although the spark for the workshop was the idea of collaborative experimentation, Mingus’ forceful personality and passionate intensity guided the group towards his vision of what jazz could be. Some musicians regarded the workshop sessions as being a “university of jazz” while others, mindful of Mingus’ relentless pursuit of perfection, dubbed them “jazz sweatshops”. The workshop process would result in many of Mingus’ classic albums including _Pithecanthropus Erectus_, _The Clown_ and his first masterpiece _Ah Um_.

### The Angry Man of Jazz
Mingus’ volatile personality and the demands he placed on both fellow musicians and his audiences led him to be nicknamed “the angry man of jazz”. There are numerous stories of Mingus’ explosive temper derailing his relationships with previously willing collaborators. In 1963 Mingus punched trombonist Jimmy Knepper so hard that he broke his teeth and he was charged with assault. It was not unheard of for Mingus to halt a concert to berate the audience for making too much noise or not paying proper attention or even to fire a musician mid-set.
While much of his anger can be explained by Mingus’ frustration in not being able to get other musicians to conform to his very particular vision of how his music should be performed it was also fed by bouts of clinical depression and, importantly, a sense of injustice that he had faced discrimination on the basis of his colour for his whole life. Though Mingus would not ally himself to any particular political group, his work during the 1960s in particular, is inherently political, imbued with righteous anger against racism and injustice. Mingus was also an outspoken critic of the music industry itself and in particular the imbalance between the musicians and their record labels often having to fight for royalties and artistic freedom. On one occasion Mingus claimed to have stormed the offices of Columbia Records dressed in a pith helmet and safari suit, brandishing a shotgun and demanding his royalties. An act he described as “creative anger”.

### Cats and Dogs
Mingus’ extraordinary autobiography _Beneath The Underdog_, published in 1971, a freewheeling mix of memoir, fantasy, musical manifesto and personal contemplation is rightly considered one of the classic jazz books. But Mingus’ literary ambitions went beyond the biography. Aside from the extensive and informative sleeve notes he provided for many of his albums, including the Grammy award winning essay “_What Is A Jazz Composer?_” which appeared on the cover of _Let My Children Hear Music_ he also published a rather unusual booklet giving guidance to toilet training cats. Offered for sale at performances or via mail-order _The Charles Mingus CAT-alog_ detailed how he managed to train his cat Nightlife to forego a litter tray and use human facilities. Mingus managed to train his cat in three or four weeks, probably showing more patience with the cat than he had with many of the musicians he worked with.

# Charles Mingus
composer
Follow Artist
One of the most important figures in 20th-century American music, CHARLES MINGUS was a virtuoso bass player, accomplished pianist, bandleader, and composer. Born in Arizona and raised in Watts, California, he studied double bass and composition in a formal way (five years with H. Rheinshagen, principal bassist of the New York Philharmonic, and compositional techniques with the legendary Lloyd Reese) while absorbing vernacular music from the great jazz masters, first-hand. His early professional experience, in the '40s, found him touring with bands like Louis Armstrong, Kid Ory, and Lionel Hampton and brought him to New York where he played and recorded with the leading musicians of the 1950s - Charlie Parker, Miles Davis, Bud Powell, Art Tatum, and Duke Ellington. One of the few bassists to do so, Mingus quickly developed as a leader of musicians, and recorded over a hundred albums and wrote over three hundred scores.
After his death in 1979 from Amyotrophic Lateral Sclerosis, the National Endowment for the Arts provided grants for a Mingus foundation called "Let My Children Hear Music," which catalogued all of Mingus' works. The microfilms of these works were then given to the Music Division of the New York Public Library, where they are currently available for study and scholarship. The Library of Congress acquired the complete Mingus Collection between 1993 and 1997, including original manuscripts, recordings, photographs, and personal memorabilia. The New Yorker wrote: "For sheer melodic and rhythmic and structural originality, his compositions may equal anything written in western music in the 20th century."

# Charles Mingus
Since Charles Mingus' death in 1979, SUE MINGUS has created and continues to direct repertory ensembles to carry on the music of her late husband. The most well-known is the Mingus Big Band, a New York institution that performs weekly to packed crowds at the Iridium nightclub. In 1989, she produced the premiere of Mingus' Epitaph at Lincoln Center's Alice Tully Hall. Other bands include the Mingus Dynasty, the original, seven-piece ensemble founded shortly after Mingus' death, and the Orchestra, a ten-piece ensemble with more classical instrumentation. She has produced numerous Grammy-nominated recordings with all three repertory bands as well as several legacy recordings, including a previously unavailable concert Charles Mingus performed with Eric Dolphy at Cornell University in 1964, available this summer on Blue Note.
Sue's memoir of her life with Mingus, Tonight At Noon, is available in paperback from DaCapo press and has been translated into several languages.

**Charles Mingus Jr.** (April 22, 1922 – January 5, 1979) was an American jazzupright bassist, composer, bandleader, pianist, and author. A major proponent of collective improvisation, he is considered one of the greatest jazz musicians and composers in history,[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Charles_Mingus#cite_note-Underdog-1) with a career spanning three decades and collaborations with other jazz greats, such as Duke Ellington, Charlie Parker, Max Roach, and Eric Dolphy. Mingus's work ranged from advanced bebop and avant-garde jazz with small and midsize ensembles to pioneering the post-bop style on seminal recordings like _Pithecanthropus Erectus_ (1956) and _Mingus Ah Um_ (1959) and progressive big band experiments such as _The Black Saint and the Sinner Lady_ (1963).

Mingus's compositions continue to be played by contemporary musicians ranging from the repertory bands Mingus Big Band, Mingus Dynasty, and Mingus Orchestra to high school students who play the charts and compete in the Charles Mingus High School Competition.[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Charles_Mingus#cite_note-2) In 1993, the Library of Congress acquired Mingus's collected papers—including scores, sound recordings, correspondence, and photos—in what it called "the most important acquisition of a manuscript collection relating to jazz in the Library's history".[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Charles_Mingus#cite_note-3)

### Early life and career
[edit]
Mingus was born in Nogales, Arizona, in 1922, to Charles Mingus Sr., a staff sergeant in the U.S. Army, and Harriet Sophia Mingus (née Phillips). His family moved to the Watts area of Los Angeles shortly after his birth.[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Charles_Mingus#cite_note-FOOTNOTESantoro2000b13%E2%80%9314-4)
Charles Sr. was born in 1877 in Swain County, North Carolina, in the Great Smoky Mountains. His mother was a white teenager, Clarinda Mingus; his father was Daniel Mingus, a farmhand and former slave who worked for Clarinda's family. Clarinda married and started a new family when he was six, leaving him in the care of her father and grandparents.[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Charles_Mingus#cite_note-5) He left home at fourteen, enlisting in the army and seeing action in the Spanish–American War. In 1917, he married Harriet Sophia Phillips, who was of mixed Chinese and African-American descent. She died of myocarditis in 1922, a few months after the birth of their son.[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Charles_Mingus#cite_note-FOOTNOTESantoro2000b14%E2%80%9317-6)

### Early life and career
Mingus was raised alongside his two elder half-sisters, from his father's first marriage. His father was married for a third time in 1923, to Mamie Carson.[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Charles_Mingus#cite_note-FOOTNOTESantoro2000b18-7) Mamie allowed only church-related music in their home, but Mingus developed an early love for other music, especially that of Duke Ellington. He studied trombone, and later cello, although he was unable to follow the cello professionally because, at the time, it was nearly impossible for a black musician to make a career of classical music, and the cello was not accepted as a jazz instrument. Despite this, Mingus remained attached to the cello; as he studied bass with Red Callender in the late 1930s, Callender even commented that the cello was still Mingus's main instrument. In his autobiography, _Beneath the Underdog_, Mingus states that he did not actually start learning bass until Buddy Collette accepted him into his swing band under the stipulation that he be the band's bass player.[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Charles_Mingus#cite_note-autogenerated1991-8)
Due to a poor education, the young Mingus could not read musical notation quickly enough to join the local youth orchestra. This had a serious impact on his early musical experiences, leaving him feeling ostracized from the classical music world. These early experiences, in addition to his lifelong confrontations with racism, were reflected in his music, which often focused on themes of racism, discrimination, and (in)justice.[[9]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Charles_Mingus#cite_note-Horton-9)
Much of the cello technique Mingus learned was applicable to double bass when he took up the instrument in high school. He studied for five years with Herman Reinshagen, principal bassist of the New York Philharmonic, and compositional techniques with Lloyd Reese.[[10]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Charles_Mingus#cite_note-10) Throughout much of his career, he played a bass made in 1927 by the German maker Ernst Heinrich Roth.

### Early life and career
Mingus was already writing relatively advanced musical pieces in his teenage years; many are similar to third stream in that they incorporate elements of classical music. A number of pieces of his were recorded in 1960 with conductor Gunther Schuller and released as _Pre-Bird_, referring to Charlie "Bird" Parker; Mingus was one of many musicians whose perspectives on music were altered by Parker into "pre- and post-Bird" eras._[citation needed_]
Mingus gained a reputation as a bass prodigy. His first major professional job was playing with former Ellington clarinetist Barney Bigard. He toured with Louis Armstrong in 1943, and by early 1945 was recording in Los Angeles in a band led by Russell Jacquet, which also included Teddy Edwards, Maurice James Simon, Wild Bill Davis, and Chico Hamilton. In May that year, in Hollywood, he was again with Edwards, in a band led by Howard McGhee.[[11]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Charles_Mingus#cite_note-11)
He then played with Lionel Hampton's band in the late 1940s; Hampton performed and recorded several Mingus pieces. In 1950–51, a popular trio of Mingus, Red Norvo and Tal Farlow, received considerable acclaim, but Mingus's race caused problems with some club owners and he left the group. Mingus was briefly a member of Ellington's band in 1953, as a substitute for bassist Wendell Marshall; however, Mingus's notorious temper led to his being one of the few musicians personally fired by Ellington ([Bubber Miley](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/James_%22Bubber%22_Miley "James \"Bubber\" Miley") and drummer Bobby Durham are among the others) after a backstage fight between Mingus and Juan Tizol.[[12]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Charles_Mingus#cite_note-FOOTNOTEHentoff197834%E2%80%9335-12)
